UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                    BEFORE THE
                      FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION


Interconnection of Large Loads to the Interstate           )                    Docket No. RM26-4-000
Transmission System                                        )


                     COMMENTS OF BLOOM ENERGY CORPORATION

        Bloom Energy Corporation (“Bloom”) submits these initial comments in response to the

U.S. Department of Energy’s (“DOE”) advanced notice of proposed rulemaking (“ANOPR”).

Also attached is a report by the Brattle Group (“Brattle”) entitled, “Accelerating Integration of

New Co-located Generation and Loads” (“Brattle Report”), which Bloom previously submitted

in the PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s (“PJM”) co-location proceeding. 1 The ANOPR presents a

major leap forward for interconnecting on-site generation and load as a composite resource. The

Commission should act expeditiously in adopting interconnection reforms.

        DOE proposes reforms that aim to meet today’s challenges resulting from surging data

center and AI infrastructure demand, while leaving it to the Commission to determine the details.

Bloom takes no position on whether the Federal Power Act provides FERC jurisdiction over

large load interconnections. However, if the Commission declines to assert jurisdiction, Bloom

urges the Commission to adopt reforms to the large generator interconnection procedures for

interconnecting on-site large load – that is, new generation co-located with large load behind the

same point of interconnection (“hybrid facilities”).

        The Commission has increasingly recognized the national security implications of AI

data centers. Both the current and prior administrations explicitly linked the advancement of AI


1
         “Comments of Bloom Energy Corporation,” Docket No. EL25-49-000, al. (filed Apr. 23, 2025) (attaching
Brattle Report).
 infrastructure to national security. 2 Accelerating the interconnection of hybrid facilities and other

reforms proposed in the ANOPR are actions the Commission can take in support of this national

security goal.

         Properly structured hybrid facility interconnection procedures will incentivize data

centers to deploy on-site generation that meets their peak loads, thereby easing resource

adequacy concerns while protecting existing customers from costs. Bloom is submitting the

Brattle Report in support of reform principles three (3), five (5), and seven (7). Brattle assesses

the concept of interconnecting new generation and co-located load as a composite facility called

an “Energy Park,” which shares the same characteristics as a hybrid facility with new generation

facilities described in the ANOPR. 3 As analyzed by Brattle, such a facility includes (i) load

designated as Network Load, (ii) co-located generation that provides primary power to load, and

(iii) controls and protection mechanisms used to limit physical withdrawals and injections to pre-

specified amounts. Like the ANOPR, Brattle finds that an integrated interconnection study

approach for new load and new generation based on requested firm withdrawals and injections

can significantly reduce the need for transmission upgrades, potentially avoiding billions in

transmission expansion costs. 4 Moreover, accelerating interconnection timelines will help meet

resource adequacy challenges from surging demand.




2
          See https://www.whitehouse.gov/presidential-actions/2025/01/removing-barriers-to-american-leadership-
in-artificial-intelligence/.
3
          While the term “Energy Park” in other contexts has previously referred to a collection of different supply
technologies (often focusing on variable energy resources), the Brattle Report gives it a different meaning. See, e.g.,
https://energyinnovation.org/wp-content/uploads/Energy-Parks-Report.pdf
4
          The ANOPR does not use the term “firm” to modify injections and withdrawals. Bloom below seeks
clarification, as that appears to be DOE’s intent.

                                                          2
        Bloom also comments on reform principles six (6) and eight (8), recommending revisions

that would strengthen the reforms and ensure that hybrid facility generators are not treated in an

unduly discriminatory manner.

I.     INTRODUCTION

       Bloom designs, manufactures and sells solid oxide fuel cell systems that utilize an

electrochemical process to convert the chemical energy in hydrogen directly to electrical energy

without combustion. The fuel cell systems power distributed energy resources that can be

located either behind-the-meter or in front-of-the-meter, which are designed in a modular fault-

tolerant format that provides critical reliability and can be designed to provide three nines

(99.9%) and five nines (99.999%) availability. Bloom has installed over 1.5 GW, of which over

400 MW power data centers. The fuel cell systems are baseload and thereby provide primary

power to customers, and also have the ability to quickly ramp up and down to follow load

fluctuations, making them an excellent option for data centers. While Bloom can install

hundreds of megawatts of dispatchable generation at a site in as little as 6 to 9 months, grid

interconnection studies and long interconnection queues often make it infeasible to meet the time

sensitive requests of large load customers.

       Bloom’s comments focus on the “bring your own generation” model and are limited to

improvements to generator interconnection procedures. Bloom assumes that hybrid facility

procedures for interconnecting generators and large load will be separate and, in the case of

hybrid facility generators, additive to the existing pro forma large generator interconnection

procedures. Bloom leaves it to others to comment on whether the Commission has jurisdiction

over large load interconnections, procedures related to such interconnections, and the

interconnection of large load with existing generation.



                                                 3
        In support of three DOE reform principles, Bloom is re-submitting the Brattle Report. As

described in the Brattle Report, a hybrid facility consists of three functional components: (i)

generation that serves as primary power for onsite supply and is subject to transmission provider

or RTO interconnection studies, (ii) co-located load, and (iii) a physical control or protection

mechanism to limit maximum flows in and out of the facility. By co-locating new primary

power (i.e., fuel cells and gas turbines), load can supply all or part of its energy and resource

adequacy on-site, thereby minimizing the impact on markets and transmission, while the

dispatchable generator can support the interconnected grid. By reflecting the controllable nature

of withdrawals and injections to the grid through one or more control and protection

mechanisms, properly structured studies that reflect the integrated nature of these resources are

less likely to identify expensive and time-consuming transmission upgrades. This approach

defines a hybrid facility under the ANOPR. Brattle demonstrates that all of this can be

accomplished while meeting reliability requirements.

       Bloom urges the Commission not only to adopt DOE’s proposal to expedite

interconnection studies where hybrid facilities agree to be curtailable and dispatchable, but also

to expedite studies where primary power serves large load and can be relied upon by load to

meet its demand. Such a “bring your own generation” model should provide a sufficient basis

for expediting interconnection studies where primary power is relied upon by the hybrid facility

load to meet its resource adequacy requirement.

       Finally, the proposal for hybrid facility generators to be responsible for 100% of

identified Network Upgrades associated with their requested injections but potentially without

cash equivalent refunds should be rejected. There is no reason to treat cash equivalent refunds

for such Network Upgrades differently from other generators that are subject to the



                                                  4
 Commission’s pro forma rules or RTO rules. In Order No. 2003-A, the Commission explained

that while the upfront payment by a generator for Network Upgrades serves as a financing

mechanism as well as a strong incentive to make efficient siting decisions, such payments were

never intended to become a means for a transmission provider to recover its costs. Although a

hybrid facility generator may cause Network Upgrades depending on its requested firm

injections to the grid, those upgrades ultimately will benefit the future transmission system by

supporting new load and generation. Given these benefits, the Commission should decline to

adopt rules that could dissuade much needed generation to serve large load by creating unduly

discriminatory cash equivalent refund rules.

II.    COMMENTS

       Bloom’s comments focus on the interconnection of large load with new generation—

specifically, the generation portion of a hybrid facility. The Commission has developed a

significant record through its technical conference on Large Loads Co-Located at Generating

Facilities in Docket No. AD24-11, and in the PJM show cause proceeding in Docket No. EL25-

49, et al., and the Commission may choose to incorporate those records in this proceeding.

       Bloom addresses the following reform principles: Principle 3 (studying hybrid facilities

together to minimize Network Upgrade costs); Principle 5 (hybrid facilities should be studied

based on the amount of injection and/or withdrawal rights requested); Principle 6 (installation of

system protection equipment to prevent unauthorized injections and withdrawals by hybrid

facilities and penalties if they occur); Principle 7 (expedited studies should be provided to hybrid

facilities that agree to be curtailable and dispatchable); and Principle 8 (hybrid facilities should

be responsible for 100% of assigned interconnection studies). Should the Commission decline

the ANOPR’s proposal to extend jurisdiction over large load interconnections, the Commission



                                                  5
 nonetheless should adopt generator interconnection procedure reforms for hybrid facility

generators consistent with the reform principles addressed below.

         A.       Reform Principle 3: Hybrid Facilities Should be Studied Together to
                  Minimize the Need for Costly Network Upgrades

         The ANOPR proposes that, to the extent practicable, the interconnection of large load

greater than 20 MW and a generator sharing the same point of interconnection be studied

together. 5 As DOE explains, “[s]uch an approach will allow for efficient siting of loads and

generating facilities and thereby minimize the need for costly network upgrades.” 6

         This reform is consistent with a principle in the Brattle Report. As previously

highlighted, the Brattle Report assesses the concept of interconnecting new generation and co-

located load as a composite facility termed an Energy Park, which is a hybrid facility. 7 Brattle

describes the process it proposes as Energy Park Integration (“EPI”) interconnection, where a

hybrid facility would be studied as a composite load and generation facility. This concept shares

similarities with the integration concept for interconnecting “Private Use Networks” in the

Electric Reliability Council of Texas, which has interconnected more than 16,000 MW of load

and co-located generation over the years.

         Because a hybrid facility supplies all or part of its load on-site, when studied as an

integrated unit both load and generation can be connected to the grid with fewer transmission

upgrades, thereby accelerating the overall interconnection process. In contrast, under current



5
         ANOPR at P 20. The ANOPR is not entirely clear here, as DOE states: “load and hybrid facilities should
be studied together with generating facilities.” However, as a hybrid facility includes a generating facility, the only
reasonable interpretation is that load and generation comprising hybrid facility be studied together.
6
         Id.
7
         While a hybrid facility could include battery storage or variable resources as its onsite resource, none of
these resources can meet the principles enunciated in the ANOPR, as they are not primary power and cannot be
combined with the load profile. Rather, it is much more likely that these resources will be sold into the market on an
as-available basis, and receive financial settlements with load.

                                                           6
 practice, where state and federal jurisdiction over interconnection differ, transmission providers

may study the new load component of a hybrid facility (without recognizing the co-located

generator), while separately studying the interconnection of new generator (without recognizing

the hybrid facility’s load). Put differently, under existing rules, load is studied as if it seeks firm

rights to withdraw 100% from the transmission system to meet its requirements, while the

generator is studied as if it seeks to inject 100% of its capacity into the transmission grid, with

some RTOs, like PJM, requiring that generator capacity also be studied for deliverability to load

throughout the system. These bifurcated, non-integrated processes ignore on-site supply benefits

and can improperly identify required Network Upgrades, resulting in slower interconnection and

unnecessarily increasing Network Upgrade costs. 8

         Brattle models the composite behavior of load and generation by accounting for three

essential components: the generator, load, and a system control mechanism that limits net

exchanges with the grid. Net load impacts would be limited to the firm nominated net grid

withdrawals, while net generator impacts would be limited to firm nominated injection levels (no

different than the ANOPR proposal, as discussed further below).

         The Brattle Report demonstrates that procedures studying hybrid facility as a single,

integrated facility can lower transmission impacts and interconnection time without sacrificing

reliability (and indeed, improving it through accelerated integration of new supply). The report

analyzes the standard contingency studies used for load reliability planning to show that the




8
         Brattle Report, p. 12-13. If the Commission declines jurisdiction over large load interconnections, it should
nevertheless urge transmission providers, RTOs, and state commissions to adopt interconnection rules to study the
load portion of a hybrid facility as a composite resource.

                                                          7
 proposed EPI approach yields lower transmission impacts even considering the contingency

cases used in transmission planning, including N-1 and N-1-1 contingency cases. 9

       The Brattle Report concludes that studying such facilities as a single resource can

accelerate interconnection by avoiding unnecessary Network Upgrades that would result from a

load-only interconnection process. 10 As Brattle finds: “By avoiding unnecessary transmission

upgrades to accommodate new large loads, the EPI process avoids any costs that would

otherwise be allocated broadly to all customers. By facilitating and accelerating a ‘bring-your-

own capacity’ approach, the proposal mitigates the resource adequacy impact of load growth,

easing price increases in the capacity market and the commensurate bill impacts for all

consumers.” 11 This approach set forth by Brattle is consistent with ANOPR reforms.

       B.        Reform Principle 5: Hybrid Facilities Should Be Studied Based on Requested
                 Grid Injections and Withdrawals

       Expanding on Principle 3, the ANOPR proposes that interconnection studies for hybrid

facilities be “based on the amount of injection and/or withdrawal rights requested,” rather than

the maximum amount of power that hypothetically can be withdrawn or injected by load or

generator, respectively, based on their gross capacity. 12

       DOE’s proposal makes sense, though the Commission should clarify that such rights refer

to “firm” withdrawal and injection rights. A generator seeking Energy Only service would be

studied as a “non-firm” resource for injection rights, while load seeking non-firm withdrawal

rights (relying on the hybrid facility generator for primary power) would be subject to similar




9
       Id. at pp. 16-20.
10
       Id. at p. 21.
11
       Id. at p. 31.
12
       ANOPR at P 22.

                                                  8
 modeling assumptions. Bloom supports DOE’s proposal with the requested clarification, as

netting would avoid unnecessary and costly upgrades.

            The Brattle Report highlights the effect of requesting Energy Only service and non-firm

withdrawal rights, which a hybrid facility comprised of a primary power source would make

possible. Brattle’s integrated reliability studies employ contingency studies based on non-firm,

net load withdrawals and generator injections, which are modeled on making wholesale sales of

energy and withdrawals of energy from the grid on a non-firm, as-feasible basis. As the Brattle

Report concludes: “By allowing non-firm injections only when the grid is available, the system

operator can take advantage of the reliability benefit of the Energy Park’s injection capability to

the extent the system needs it and can reliably accommodate it, without needing to undertake

costly transmission upgrades.” 13 Withdrawals from the grid likewise can be modeled on an as-

available basis because protection systems can be in place to ensure that the maximum non-firm

withdrawal level for reliability reasons cannot be exceeded at any time. Even under contingency

conditions, reliability can be ensured assuming a rapid ramp rate from the hybrid facility’s

generator (typical of solid oxide fuel cell systems) and control by the system operator via

Security Constrained Economic Dispatch in the real-time market. 14

            C.        Reform Principle 6: Hybrid Interconnections Must Install System Protection
                      Equipment to Prevent Unauthorized Injections or Withdrawals

            This principle requires hybrid facilities to install system protection facilities to prevent

unauthorized injections or withdrawals. 15 The ANOPR seeks comments on minimum technical




13
            Brattle Report at p. 13. The Brattle Report goes on to model and demonstrate how this can be done
reliably.
14
            Id. at p. 17.
15
            ANOPR at P 23.

                                                           9
 requirements and whether penalties should be mandated for unauthorized injections or

withdrawals.

       The scope of the term “unauthorized” must be addressed. Bloom urges the Commission

to distinguish between inadvertent or transient injections (authorized injections), and sustained or

intentional injections that result in malfunction or non-compliance with transmission provider or

RTO directives (unauthorized injections).

       Inadvertent or transient injections by a hybrid facility generator should be worked out on

a bilateral basis with the transmission provider or RTO undertaking the studies. Bloom, for

example, has engineered in front-of-the-meter fuel cell systems (load and generation

interconnecting to the same point of interconnection), where Bloom has installed reverse power

relays tied to a curtailment protocol to prevent power flows to the grid beyond inadvertent or

transient flows. Because the generating facility is grid following (with the generator following

load fluctuations and the amount of load not otherwise served by system power), a certain

limited amount of energy may flow onto the grid due to delays in relaying, controls, and

curtailment response. The permissible magnitude and duration of reverse or unauthorized power

flows are system-dependent and must be coordinated with the transmission provider or RTO,

considering grid strength, local protection settings, and inverter control response times.

       Among the issues that must be coordinated is how “inadvertent” flows should be

addressed if load curtails to zero without notice. Under such circumstances, the generator will

continue to produce and inject energy onto the grid for a number of cycles. The number of

permissible cycles or seconds before the generation facility is taken (or forced) offline must be

determined by the transmission provider or RTO based on what the grid can readily absorb at the

point of interconnection. Any minimum technical requirements should be consistent with



                                                 10
 existing standards, such as IEEE 1547-2018 and emerging NERC IBR performance and

modeling guidelines to avoid duplicative or conflicting requirements.

        Regarding penalties, if adopted, they should be limited to intentional injections resulting

in malfunction or non-compliance with transmission provider or RTO directives. Adopting

prescriptive requirements with penalties may not accord with differences among transmission

providers and the grids they operate. It would be unreasonable to adopt penalties for inadvertent

or transient injections that are unavoidable and which the transmission provider or RTO has

concluded are allowable or authorized.

        D.       Reform Principle 7: Expedited Studies Should Be Provided to Hybrid
                 Facilities that Agree to be Curtailable and Dispatchable

        The ANOPR would provide for expedited interconnection studies of hybrid facilities so

long as they are both curtailable and dispatchable, respectively. 16 Bloom urges the Commission

to expand expedited studies to include hybrid facilities having primary power sufficient to meet

its peak load. The Commission may also wish to expedite studies more generally where initial

studies indicate that no Network Upgrades are needed, consistent with a recent proposal by the

Southwest Power Pool, Inc. (“SPP”). 17

        The ANOPR’s underlying theory is sound. Dispatchable on-site generation, such as fuel

cells, can self-supply the hybrid facility’s load when (i) the grid is not available, (ii) the price of

grid withdrawals by load is not advantageous, or (iii) under terms of the hybrid facility PPA, load

does not need the full output of the on-site generator during off-peak times. Accordingly, in

addition to providing resource adequacy to co-located load, hybrid facility generators can




16
        Id. at P 24.
17
        See Southwest Power Pool, Inc., Docket No. ER26-247-000 (filed Oct. 24, 2025).

                                                     11
 dispatch power to the grid and provide a valuable reliability contribution based on available net

injections. 18

        While hybrid facility generators are readily dispatchable, load may choose to forgo being

treated as a curtailable demand resource. Stakeholder comments in the PJM large load additions

process have opposed mandatory curtailment. The ANOPR seemingly takes the position that

agreement by a hybrid facility to be dispatchable and curtailable is the “grand bargain” for

expedited interconnection studies, but it should not be the only way to receive expedited studies.

        It is similarly reasonable to provide for expedited interconnection studies based on the

need for Network Upgrades and further studies. For example, where primary power in a hybrid

facility is capable of serving 100% of its load, Network Upgrades likely will be avoided and

there is no reason to create a multi-year interconnection queue for such projects, even where load

does not agree to be curtailable demand resource. As Brattle points out, in such cases rather than

expansive interconnection studies, it would be appropriate for the transmission provider/RTO to

assess non-firm net injections similarly to Surplus Interconnection Service studies. 19 These

studies are expedited by many transmission providers and RTOs today, and there is no reason

they should not similarly be expedited for hybrid facility load seeking non-firm withdrawals,

assuming the Commission finds jurisdiction to exist.

        The ANOPR also seeks comment on the appropriate timeline for conducting studies.

Bloom notes that SPP’s recently filed High Impact Large Load plus generation proposal would

complete interconnection studies in 90 days, provided the need for additional reliability studies

are not identified. 20 Consistent with existing reliability study requirements for Surplus

 Interconnection Service, a 90-day period to study hybrid facilities seems reasonable, provided

requested withdrawal and injection rights do not identify the need for additional reliability

studies to determine if Network Upgrades are required. Additionally, the Commission in a final

rule could justify expedited interconnection studies for hybrid facilities based on the identified

national security needs regarding data centers and AI infrastructure, as discussed above.

        E.       Reform Principle 8: Hybrid Facilities Should be Responsible for 100% of
                 Network Upgrades Assigned Through Interconnection Studies, Potentially
                 Without Receiving Future Credits

        The ANOPR proposes that hybrid facilities be responsible for 100% of identified

Network Upgrade costs, and seeks comments on whether there should be any crediting

mechanism. Bloom’s comments focus only on Network Upgrade cost responsibility based on

requested generator injections and the appropriateness of retaining “cash equivalent refunds” for

such upgrades consistent with Commission precedent.

        The concept of participant funding for Network Upgrades is not new in the context of

generator interconnections. Bloom urges the Commission to consider the expansive record and

orders on participant funding developed more than two decades ago in Docket No. RM02-1. 21

These policies remain relevant for the interconnection of generation as a hybrid facility. 22

          Bloom acknowledges that some states and public utility commissions have passed laws and tariffs requiring
large load to be responsible for paying 100% of Network Upgrade costs resulting from their interconnection. If the
Commission asserts jurisdiction over large load interconnections, as proposed in the ANOPR, the Commission
likewise may have to address what level of comity it will grant to these state policies. While Bloom does not take
any position on the interconnection of large load alone, where a FERC-jurisdictional generator is interconnected as
part of a hybrid facility, crediting policies initially developed in Order No. 2003 ought to continue.

                                                        13
          The Commission has long held that non-independent transmission providers do not have

leeway on how they handle crediting/repayment of upfront payments by an interconnection

customer for Network Upgrades, while RTOs have developed differing policies that apply

equally to all generators subject to large generator interconnection procedures. For generator

interconnections subject to the Commission’s pro forma policies, although Network Upgrades

are funded by interconnection customers (unless the transmission provider elects to fund them),

interconnection customers are thereafter entitled to cash equivalent refunds (i.e., transmission

credits or cash refunds) repaid over a period of time equal to the amount paid for downstream

Network Upgrades. 23 In Order No. 2003-A, the Commission reasoned that crediting for an

upfront payment is appropriate because the payment “serves not as a rate for interconnection or

transmission service, but simply as a financing mechanism that is designed to facilitate the

efficient construction of Network Upgrades.” 24 As the Commission explained:

         The purpose of the upfront financial payment is twofold. First, by providing the
         Transmission Provider with a source of funds to construct the Network Upgrades,
         the upfront payment by the Interconnection Customer alleviates any delay that
         might result if the Transmission Provider were forced to secure funding
         elsewhere. Second, by placing the Interconnection Customer initially at risk for
         the full cost of the Network Upgrades, the upfront payment provides the
         Interconnection Customer with a strong incentive to make efficient siting
         decisions and, in general, to make good faith requests for Interconnection Service.
         However, the upfront payment is not a rate for service, and thus is not intended to
         be the means by which the Transmission Provider recovers the cost of the
         Network Upgrades. Rather, the Transmission Provider's right to charge for
         transmission service at the higher of an embedded cost rate, or an incremental rate
         designed to recover the cost of the Network Upgrades, provides the Transmission
         Provider with a cost recovery mechanism that ensures that native load and other
         transmission customers will not subsidize service to the Interconnection
         Customer. 25

 The Commission re-affirmed this policy in Order No. 2003-B, stating, “[d]espite the unsupported

hypothetical generalizations of some petitioners, we have not been presented with any evidence

that native load and other Transmission Customers cannot be held harmless under our existing

pricing policy.” 26 The Commission concluded that if a transmission provider (or existing

transmission customer) believes transmission customers are not held harmless under this policy,

a “demonstration in an actual transmission rate filing” can be made. 27

       With respect to hybrid facility generators, Bloom urges the Commission to retain the

existing cash equivalent refund policies that apply to other new generation interconnecting with

non-independent transmission providers and RTO systems. Treating a hybrid facility generator

differently than other generation subject to FERC jurisdiction would be unduly discriminatory.

If the transmission provider or RTO believes that existing customers are not being held harmless

through the crediting mechanism, they (or other customers) are free, as the Commission

concluded in Order No. 2003-B, to make a case-specific demonstration at FERC.

III.   CONCLUSION

       For the foregoing reasons, Bloom urges the Commission to adopt the above-discussed

reform principles for hybrid facility generators, together with the modifications discussed herein.

If the Commission declines the ANOPR’s proposal to assert jurisdiction over large load

interconnections, Bloom nevertheless urges the Commission to adopt large generator

interconnection procedure reforms associated with interconnecting hybrid facility

 Executive Summary
    _________

Faster connection of large loads for artificial intelligence has been identified as a federal
priority. Many new large loads such as data centers are applying to connect to the grid in PJM
and elsewhere, creating opportunities for economic growth and higher utilization of electrical
infrastructure.

This load growth is challenging both transmission and resource adequacy. In some cases, new
large loads exceed existing transmission capacity, and new customers must wait while
(potentially costly) transmission upgrades are made. In other cases, load growth exceeds
projected additions of generating capacity. In many areas, concerns have been raised regarding
the affordability implications for consumers of these transmission and capacity impacts from
growth in large loads. The co-location of such loads with generation has emerged as one
solution to address these transmission and resource adequacy challenges.1 PJM
Interconnection L.L.C. (PJM) recently validated co-location as a possible solution in its Answer
to the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) in Docket No. EL25-49-000.2

In this report we assess the concept of connecting new generation and co-located load as a
composite facility called an “Energy Park.” This approach can significantly reduce the need for
new transmission while accelerating integration of new loads together with new generation
resources that can ease resource adequacy concerns, reducing costly resource and grid
investments and mitigating bill impacts for consumers. We assess current processes in PJM and
identify possible reforms necessary to facilitate the interconnection of such Energy Parks.

The key findings in our study are as follows:

     1. Integrated Energy Park interconnection is a practical way to quickly connect large
        loads with fewer transmission upgrades

 Energy Parks connected to the transmission system consist of three components: generation,
co-located load, and a mechanism to control flows into or out of the Energy Park at the point of
interconnection (POI) with the transmission grid. Following the interconnection approach for
Private Use Networks (PUNs) used in the Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT), we
describe an Energy Park Integration (EPI) process that would study the Energy Park as a
composite load and generation facility (at smaller scale referred to as a “micro grid”), instead of
separately studying the load in one process and the generator in another. 3

We illustrate stylized contingency cases (such as shown in Figure ES-1 below) that are used in
reliability studies to show how an Energy Park studied as a composite facility can be connected
to the grid more quickly and less expensively due to lower transmission upgrades relative to a
conventional study approach. This is because, in the conventional approach, PJM and the
transmission owner separately evaluate generation and load components respectively without
consideration of the self-balancing effect of co-located generation on co-located load, and
potentially ignore the action of a control system (and system protection mechanism) that limits
Energy Park power flows to and from the grid to specified levels.

In all cases where the grid connection of the Energy Park itself is smaller than the Energy Park’s
load and generation, the park’s embedded generation—such as a combination of fuel cells,
natural gas resources, battery storage, and variable resources—would serve as the primary
generation source supplying the relevant portion of the Energy Park’s load. For the portion of
Energy Park load that can be served from the grid, the embedded generation would both be
dispatchable into the regional market and serve as backup generation for the Energy Park load.4

addition to meeting backup power needs, it can also serve as primary generation to self-supply

incentivizing new large load customers to bring their own new generation, the proposed
integrated Energy Park interconnection process offers a solution that can more quickly

In summary, EPI is practical, addresses resource adequacy and grid challenges, and offers
significant benefits if the Energy Park resources are dispatchable on as-needed basis. The

self-supply all or a portion of Energy Park loads, thereby mitigating the resource adequacy and

PJM, the Regional Transmission Organization (RTO) serving 13 states and the District of
Columbia, forecasts rapid growth in electricity demand, driven in large part by expansion of
planned data centers and other large loads.9 Transmission infrastructure and resource
adequacy are being strained to integrate the new loads. In some cases, new large loads must
wait years while time-consuming and costly transmission upgrades are made.10 Importantly,
PJM has expressed significant concerns over resource adequacy challenges.11

Speed to market is a critical motivation for many new large data center customers, as the ability
to launch new services and scale operations is critical to competitiveness. There has therefore
been interest in co-locating loads with existing generation instead of going through a lengthy
load integration process.12 PJM has cited nearly 8.5 GW of large loads (including data centers)
that have requested to interconnect in co-location arrangements with existing generators.13
Co-locating load with existing generation could avoid the need for time-consuming network
upgrades prior to connection, but raises a variety of questions (such as cost allocation) that are
beyond the scope of this report. Co-location of new loads with existing generation also
exacerbates PJM’s resource adequacy concerns and can cause transmission reliability issues by
effectively adding new large load without a corresponding increase in local supply or
transmission capability.

As shown below, because an Energy Park locally supplies all or part of its load, it can be
connected to the grid with fewer transmission upgrades (and thus more quickly) when it is
studied as an integrated unit. By contrast, using the existing separated processes to study the
new load component of an Energy Park (without recognizing the co-located generation) while
studying the new generation (without recognizing the co-located load) will ignore these self-
supply benefits and overstate the necessary transmission upgrades, slowing down
interconnection and unnecessarily increasing costs.

The proposed EPI approach models the composite behavior of load and generation in an Energy
Park by accounting for its three essential components: generators, load, and a control
mechanism that limits net exchanges with the grid.

For example, as shown in Figure 1 above, consider an Energy Park with 500 MW of load; on-site
primary generation totaling 550 MW of installed capacity (e.g., composed of approximately
1,700 individual generation units of 325 kW each to ensure high availability for on-site supply in
case of maintenance or other unit outages, such as Bloom Energy’s 325 kW individual Energy
Server systems); and a control mechanism that limits net grid withdrawals to less than 340 MW
and (non-firm) net grid injections to less than 50 MW. The EPI study approach would model
both the Energy Park generation and load online in the base load study case. Studied net load
impacts would be limited to just the maximum net grid withdrawal at the Energy Park (340 MW
net withdrawal in the example), while assessed net injection impacts from the generation
would be limited to the maximum possible injection level (50 MW).

By contrast, if today’s studies are performed separately on the generation or load component
in isolation, they will analyze reliability needs to accommodate up to 500 MW of withdrawals
from the grid and 550 MW of injections into the grid, as highlighted in the New Option 6
requirement that a co-located generator have firm CIRs. In other words, the integration study
of the Energy Park load would have no mechanism to simultaneously consider the co-located
Energy Park generation (which would be represented in a separate process, the PJM generation
interconnection queue), leading PJM to model a 550 MW base case injection and the

         Conclusion
         _________

We have described an EPI process that can accelerate the integration of Energy Parks consisting
of co-located load, primary generation, and a control mechanism that regulates grid
withdrawals and injections. We illustrate with stylized N-1 and N-1-1 contingency scenarios
how EPI studies allow grid planners to leverage an Energy Park’s generation and control
mechanism that limit net withdrawals to those serviceable by the grid with minimal upgrades.
We identify the reforms necessary to enable new large loads and co-located generation to
interconnect quickly under the EPI framework. Namely: establishing EPI protocols; clarifying the
role of the grid operator and transmission owners; allowing for an expedited study process and
assessment protocol that reflects the lower expected grid impact of Energy Parks; and
integrating the dispatchability of the Energy Park’s assets in real-time operational frameworks
(SCED or otherwise) to maximize their benefits for grid reliability and economic dispatch of
available resources. An accelerated interconnection process under the EPI framework offers the
opportunity to support federal and state priorities on data centers, manufacturing, and artificial
intelligence infrastructure and addresses critical challenges with resource adequacy and grid
upgrades. In particular, the benefits of the proposed EPI framework are as follows:

ACCELERATES INTERCONNECTION OF NEW LOAD AND NEW GENERATION

Eliminating network upgrades through controllable Energy Parks can immediately reduce large
